newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr seen treading water after G7 meeting - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Dlr seen treading water after G7 meeting - dealers.

text.p: The dollar is likely to tread water against the yen for the near term, dealers said, after officials at the weekend's G7 meeting indicated a desire for currency stability and said the dollar has surged enough.
"The market did not anticipate the comments saying that the reversal of the dollar had ended," said Takashi Kanagami, deputy general manager at Mitsubishi Trust and Banking.
"The agreement, which might have been intended to stabilise the dollar/yen rate at 120 to 125 yen, may have the effect of checking the dollar's rise," he added.
"We believe that major misalignments in exchange markets...have been corrected," a statement issued after the talks among Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers and central bankers on Saturday said.
The dollar rose as high as 122.85 yen on Monday in early Tokyo trade on a flood of dollar buying by Japanese importers, after falling earlier in Asian trade to about 120.30 yen.

"Given the greater volatility in the dollar/yen rate compared to the dollar/mark, there may have been some agreement (between Japan and the U.S.)," said Ryohei Muramatsu, manager of treasury and foreign exchange at Commerzbank.
An apparent subtle change in U.S. currency policy caught many traders off guard on Friday in New York and made participants cautious on Monday in Tokyo.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Friday that the dollar has been strong "for some time now."
Traders found a subtle change in comments by Rubin who had repeately said before that a strong dollar was in the U.S. interest.
"The market is becoming sceptical of the U.S. strong dollar policy after Rubin's remarks (on Friday)," said Commerzbank's Muramatsu.

"I think (change lies) with the U.S. side -- but the U.S. will maintain a strong dollar. They just want to moderate exchange and interest rates. There's no indication they're willing to back it up with real policy changes," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Dealers said a drastic change in the U.S. dollar policy was unlikely because such a move would reduce demand for U.S. assets and risk hurting the U.S. financial markets seriously.
Wataru Ito, deputy general manager at Sanwa Bank Ltd, said the United Sates had imposed several tasks on Japan in return for its endorsement of calls by Japan to stabilise the market.
"But if Japan fails to carry out various reforms in its budget, stock market and tax system smoothly, there may be the risk that the yen will be sold further," he added.
Participants here were mixed as to whether the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will sell dollars for yen in the open market if the yen resumes its fall to over 125 yen to the dollar.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Monday that Japan's view on currencies is reflected in the G7 statement, comments which were echoed by Japan's chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama on Monday morning.
Mitsuzuka, speaking in parliament, added that the G7 countries also agreed on Japan's view that cooperation among the group should be maintained.
"There is a possibility that Japan alone will sell dollars to stem the yen's falls," said Commerzbank's Muramatsu, but added that concerted intervention was unlikely to take place.
